## Introduction

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children with type 1 diabetes. Pediatric DKA commonly occurs at the time of diagnosis or initial presentation of type 1 diabetes. DKA develops when circulating insulin levels fall, either relatively or absolutely, while counterregulatory hormones increase. This hormonal imbalance amplifies normal metabolic processes, leading to an exaggerated physiologic response, causing hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, ketosis, and acidosis.[1]

According to the International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes, the biochemical criteria for the diagnosis of DKA are the presence of all of the following in a patient with diabetes:

Hyperglycemia: Blood glucose >200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L)

Metabolic acidosis: Venous pH <7.3 (or) serum bicarbonate < 15 mEq/L (15 mmol/L)

Ketonemia: Presence of ketones in the blood (>3 mmol/L beta-hydroxybutyrate) or "moderate or large" ketones [1][2][3]

## Etiology

DKA develops from an absolute or relative deficiency of insulin accompanied by increased concentrations of counterregulatory hormones, including catecholamines, glucagon, cortisol, and growth hormone (see Image. Pathophysiology of DKA).[4] This hormonal imbalance produces a pronounced catabolic state that disrupts normal glucose and lipid metabolism.

Insulin deficiency and elevated counterregulatory hormones increase hepatic and renal glucose production through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis while simultaneously reducing peripheral glucose utilization. These metabolic changes produce progressive hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality. Increased lipolysis releases free fatty acids, which undergo hepatic ketogenesis, generating ketone bodies and resulting in ketonemia and metabolic acidosis.[5][6][7][3] As circulating ketone levels increase, osmotic diuresis promotes substantial water and electrolyte losses, resulting in progressive dehydration. Vomiting can further intensify these losses. Without timely administration of exogenous insulin and appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, the metabolic disturbance can progress to severe dehydration and potentially life-threatening metabolic acidosis.[5]

When circulating glucose becomes insufficient or cannot be effectively utilized by cells due to inadequate insulin, ketone bodies become an important alternative energy source for the brain. Because the brain has limited capacity to store fuel, it relies primarily on circulating glucose and ketones to meet its energy requirements. Consequently, the metabolic alterations accompanying DKA can rapidly affect neurologic function when treatment does not restore metabolic stability.

The severity of DKA is categorized according to the degree of metabolic acidosis (see Table. Severity of DKA). This classification provides an important framework for assessing disease severity, guiding treatment intensity, and determining the level of monitoring required during management.

Severity | PH | Bicarbonate
Mild | < 7.3 | 10-15 mmol/L
Moderate | < 7.2 | 5-9 mmol/L
Severe | < 7.2 | < 5 mmol/L

## History and Physical

Clinical Assessment

The classic clinical manifestations of DKA include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss. Careful history-taking and a comprehensive physical examination remain essential for recognizing DKA promptly and minimizing the risk of misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis in children.[1] Clinical manifestations can progress rapidly and may include vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, weakness, and lethargy. Abdominal discomfort and ileus can develop because of potassium depletion, metabolic acidosis, and reduced splanchnic perfusion. During early DKA, abdominal pain may become sufficiently severe to mimic an acute abdomen, potentially complicating the initial clinical assessment.[1]

Dehydration may present with tachycardia, delayed capillary refill time, poor skin turgor, and dry mucous membranes. Metabolic acidosis can produce Kussmaul breathing, characterized by rapid, deep respirations, along with a fruity odor to the breath. Cerebral edema represents a serious neurologic complication, and warning signs of evolving neurologic injury include headache, bradycardia, irritability, increasing drowsiness, altered mental status, cranial nerve deficits, new focal neurologic findings, hypertension, decreased responsiveness, and coma. Clinicians can use the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) to assess and monitor changes in mental status objectively.[17]

The initial clinical assessment should include evaluation for signs of infection and other potential precipitating causes of DKA. Clinicians should identify and treat any underlying infection or other precipitating condition as clinically indicated. Accurate measurement of the patient’s weight remains essential because weight-based calculations determine appropriate doses of insulin and other medications. Clinicians should promptly identify potential precipitating factors for DKA, including intercurrent infection, insulin pump failure, medication or substance use, and pregnancy. Recognition of these triggers supports timely treatment of the underlying cause and may reduce the risk of persistent metabolic deterioration or recurrent DKA.
